summary: Describes how PGP can be used to provide privacy and authentication for email using the MIME security content types. It lets mail programs encrypt and sign messages in a standard MIME structure.

plainLanguage.summary: MIME is the format that lets one email message carry different kinds of part, such as text, pictures and attachments. This RFC says how to use MIME to carry two things made by PGP: a signed version of the message and an encrypted version of it. The signature and the encrypted text each sit in their own part of the message, so a mail program can find them without understanding PGP itself.

questions: how to use pgp with mime
how to encrypt email with pgp
subtitle: How to wrap PGP-encrypted and PGP-signed data inside standard MIME email messages.

tldr.problem: Earlier ways of mixing PGP with MIME email, including the withdrawn application/pgp content type, made it impossible to recover a signed message body without parsing PGP-specific data structures.
tldr.mechanism: It uses the multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted formats from RFC 1847 and defines three content types: application/pgp-encrypted, application/pgp-signature and application/pgp-keys. The signed text and the signature travel in separate body parts.
tldr.outcome: Mail programs get a standard way to carry PGP privacy and authentication. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 3156.

today: RFC 2015 is a Proposed Standard published in October 1996 and has since been updated by RFC 3156, so read that RFC alongside it. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Previous work on integrating PGP with MIME, including the since withdrawn application/pgp content type, suffered from a number of problems. The most significant was the inability to recover signed message bodies without parsing data structures specific to PGP.

This work makes use of the solution proposed in RFC 1847, which defines security multipart formats for MIME. The security multiparts clearly separate the signed message body from the signature, and have a number of other desirable properties. The document is styled after RFC 1848, which defines MIME Object Security Services for providing security and authentication.

The document defines three new content types for implementing security and privacy with PGP: application/pgp-encrypted, application/pgp-signature and application/pgp-keys.
sections.plainLanguage: MIME lets one email message carry different kinds of part, such as text, pictures and attachments. This RFC says how to use MIME to carry two things made by PGP: a signed version of the message and an encrypted version of it. The signature and the encrypted text each sit in their own part, so a mail program can find them without understanding PGP itself.

sections.title: PGP Data Formats and Transfer Encoding
sections.content:
PGP can generate either ASCII armor or 8-bit binary output when encrypting data, generating a digital signature, or extracting public key data. The ASCII armor output is the REQUIRED method for data transfer. This allows those users who do not have the means to interpret the formats described in this document to be able to extract and use the PGP information in the message.

When the amount of data to be transmitted requires that it be sent in many parts, the MIME message/partial mechanism should be used rather than the multipart ASCII armor PGP format.

Multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted are to be treated by agents as opaque, meaning that the data is not to be altered in any way. However, many existing mail gateways will detect if the next hop does not support MIME or 8-bit data and perform conversion to either Quoted-Printable or Base64. This presents serious problems for multipart/signed, in particular, where the signature is invalidated when such an operation occurs. For this reason all data signed according to this protocol MUST be constrained to 7 bits, and 8-bit data should be encoded using either Quoted-Printable or Base64. This also includes the case where a signed object is also encrypted. The restriction increases the likelihood that the signature will be valid upon receipt.

Data that is only to be encrypted is allowed to contain 8-bit characters and therefore need not be converted to a 7-bit format. The implementor's note repeats MIME's advice to "be conservative in what you generate, and liberal in what you accept": an implementation should accept messages with any content-transfer-encoding, but restrict generation to the 7-bit format required by this memo, so that future compatibility is possible in the event the Internet SMTP framework becomes 8-bit friendly.
sections.plainLanguage: PGP data travels as text in ASCII armor rather than as raw binary, so that a person can still read it. Signed text must be limited to seven bits per character, because a mail gateway that converts text to Base64 or Quoted-Printable would break the signature. Text that is only encrypted has no such limit.

sections.title: PGP Encrypted Data
sections.content:
Before encryption with PGP, the data should be written in MIME canonical format, covering both body and headers.

PGP encrypted data is denoted by the multipart/encrypted content type, and MUST have a protocol parameter value of "application/pgp-encrypted". The value of the parameter MUST be enclosed in quotes.

The multipart/encrypted MUST consist of exactly two parts. The first MIME body part must have a content type of application/pgp-encrypted, and it contains the control information. A message complying with this standard MUST contain a Version: 1 field in this body. Since the PGP packet format contains all other information necessary for decrypting, no other information is required here.

The second MIME body part MUST contain the actual encrypted data, and must be labeled with a content type of application/octet-stream.
sections.plainLanguage: An encrypted message has exactly two parts. The first is a small control part that says only "Version: 1". The second holds the encrypted bytes, written as a PGP ASCII-armored message.

sections.title: PGP Signed Data
sections.content:
PGP signed messages are denoted by the multipart/signed content type, with a protocol parameter which MUST have a value of "application/pgp-signature" and MUST be quoted. The micalg parameter MUST have a value of pgp-<hash-symbol>, where the hash symbol identifies the message integrity check used to generate the signature. The currently defined values are md5 for the MD5 checksum and sha1 for the SHA.1 algorithm.

The multipart/signed body MUST consist of exactly two parts. The first part contains the signed data in MIME canonical format, including a set of appropriate content headers describing the data. The second body MUST contain the PGP digital signature and must be labeled with a content type of application/pgp-signature.

When the PGP digital signature is generated, the data to be signed must first be converted to its type or subtype specific canonical form. For text/plain this means conversion to an appropriate character set and conversion of line endings to the canonical <CR><LF> sequence. An appropriate Content-Transfer-Encoding is then applied, and each line of the encoded data MUST end with the canonical <CR><LF> sequence. MIME content headers are then added to the body, each ending with the same sequence. The digital signature MUST be calculated over both the data to be signed and its set of content headers, and it MUST be generated detached from the signed data, so that the process does not alter the signed data in any way.

Upon receipt of a signed message, an application MUST convert line endings to the canonical <CR><LF> sequence before the signature can be verified, since the local mail transfer agent may have converted to a local end of line convention. It MUST then pass both the signed data and its associated content headers, along with the PGP signature, to the signature verification service.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed message has exactly two parts as well: the text that was signed, and the signature itself. The signature covers the text and the headers that describe it, so the receiver has to reproduce the same line endings before checking it.

sections.title: Encrypted and Signed Data
sections.content:
Sometimes it is desirable to both digitally sign and then encrypt a message. This protocol allows two methods of doing so.

The first is the RFC 1847 encapsulation: the data is first signed as a multipart/signed body, and then encrypted to form the final multipart/encrypted body. In other words, the signed multipart is placed inside the encrypted one, and the encrypted PGP message holds the whole signed structure.

The second is the combined method. Versions 2.x of PGP allow data to be signed and encrypted in one operation. This method is an acceptable shortcut, and has the benefit of less overhead. The resulting data should be formed as a multipart/encrypted object. Messages which are encrypted and signed in this combined fashion are REQUIRED to follow the same canonicalization rules as for multipart/signed objects. It is explicitly allowed for an agent to decrypt a combined message and rewrite it as a multipart/signed object using the signature data embedded in the encrypted version.
sections.plainLanguage: A message can be signed and then encrypted, or signed and encrypted in one step. Either way the outer shape is the same encrypted multipart, and either way the text has to be put in its canonical form before the signature is made.

sections.title: Distribution of PGP Public Keys
sections.content: The document defines one more content type, application/pgp-keys, with no required parameters and no optional parameters. This is the content type which should be used for relaying public key blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: Public keys travel as their own content type, application/pgp-keys, so that a key can be sent inside an ordinary email message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Use of this protocol has the same security considerations as PGP, and is not known to either increase or decrease the security of messages using it. The document points at the PGP message exchange format specification for more information.

The document also records that PGP and Pretty Good Privacy are trademarks of Philip Zimmermann.
sections.plainLanguage: Wrapping PGP in MIME does not make a message safer or less safe than PGP itself. Everything that is true about PGP's security is still true here.
